info.name: Yatra 2.0 — API
info.description:
Yatra 2.0 — domestic flight booking platform for Nepal (CPJ119 Advanced Java).

## What is in here

| Folder | Contents |
|---|---|
| **00 · Setup** | Sign in (captures the Bearer token), the demo `reset` then `seed`, sign in again (the reset rebuilds the administrator, so its id is re-captured), then sign in as a customer. Run these first, in that order — everything under `/api/admin/**` needs a token. |
| **Admin · Airlines** | the airline CRUD, the logo bytes endpoint (`ETag` + a conditional `304`) and its failure cases. |
| **Admin · Destinations** | the Cloudinary upload, the destination CRUD, and the two list paths (admin + public) that share one body. |
| **Admin · Flights** | the flight CRUD, the seat map it generates (a public read), the filters, and the route/airline validation failures. |
| **Public · Booking write (Phase 6)** | `POST /api/bookings` — the wizard's own write, and the seat hold it leaves behind. |
| **Admin · Bookings (Phase 9)** | `GET /api/admin/bookings` (search, filters, paging), `GET /api/admin/bookings/{id}`, `PUT /api/admin/bookings/{id}/status` — success and failure cases. |
| **Payments (Phase 10)** | the eSewa gateway walk (`initiate` → `verify`, success **and** declined), the admin payments ledger, its filters and paging, and the refund. |
| **Admin · Users (Phase 11)** | the user roster (search, filters, paging), create, edit, activate/deactivate, delete — the `ADMIN_ACCOUNT_PROTECTED` and `USER_HAS_BOOKINGS` refusals, and the per-account booking read behind them. |
| **Admin · Tickets (Phase 12)** | the issued-ticket read: search by PNR / ticket number / customer / flight / booking id, the page's booking-status dropdown, the ticket's own `ISSUED` / `CANCELLED`, paging, the detail read and its 404, and both layers of the admin guard. |
| **Admin · Dashboard (Phase 13)** | the dashboard read: the two keys the page renders (`bookings` + the seven §2.5 `stats` cards), and the four cross-checks that compare each card against the endpoint listing the same table — plus both layers of the admin guard. |
| **99 · Delete guards** | why a flight, airline or destination that is in use refuses to be deleted — and the *disable it instead* path that does work. |

**Run order matters, and the folders are arranged for it.** A collection run walks airlines → destinations → flights → booking write → Phase 9 → payments → Phase 11 → tickets (Phase 12) → the dashboard (Phase 13) → the delete guards, which is also the order the modules depend on each other. Each create captures the id the next folder needs (`{{airlineId}}` → `{{newCodeFrom}}`/`{{newCodeTo}}` → `{{flightId}}` → `{{pendingBookingId}}`), so nothing is pasted between tabs by hand.

**The tickets module joined it at Phase 12, and the dashboard at Phase 13** — see those folders. Phase 13 is the one folder that asserts almost nothing about its own endpoint in isolation: it reads the four other lists and checks that the cards agree with them, because the roadmap's checkpoint for a dashboard is that its numbers match the database rather than that the body has the right keys. What is still not here is the auth surface beyond the two sign-ins (register, refresh). The registration confirmation email (Phase 11's other half) needs a real mailbox and is described in the Users folder.

## How to use it

1. Start the app (`./mvnw spring-boot:run` in IntelliJ or the terminal) and import **both** files from `postman/`.
2. Select the **Yatra 2.0 — local** environment (top-right). `baseUrl` defaults to `http://localhost:8080`; the collection carries the same defaults, so it also works with no environment selected.

> **Where each value lives, and why it matters.** The environment holds only what a human configures (`baseUrl`, the demo account). The transient values — `{{adminToken}}`, `{{userToken}}`, the ids every create captures (`{{airlineId}}`, `{{destIdFrom}}`, `{{flightId}}`, `{{bookingId}}`, `{{pendingBookingId}}`), the codes it generates (`{{newIata}}`, `{{newCodeFrom}}`, `{{newFlightNo}}`) and `{{today}}` — are **collection** variables on purpose: Postman resolves an environment variable *before* a collection variable, so an `adminToken` defined in the environment would shadow the one the sign-in request captures and every admin call would go out with an empty Bearer token.
3. Run **00 · Setup**, in order: **Sign in (admin)** → **Reset the demo data** → **Seed the demo data** → **Sign in (admin) again** → **Sign in (customer)**. The sign-in requests store their tokens in `{{adminToken}}` / `{{userToken}}` automatically — every admin request sends the token as a Bearer header, and nothing else needs copying between tabs.

## Booting from an empty database (the circle you will hit)

`POST /api/admin/seed` is admin-only, and the `admin@yatra.com` account the sign-in uses is **created by that seed** — so on a database that has never been seeded there is no admin to authorise the first seed. Registering does not close the circle either: `POST /api/auth/register` creates a `USER`.

One manual step, once per database:

1. `POST /api/auth/register` (that endpoint is public — from Signup, or by hand).
2. `UPDATE users SET role = 'ADMIN' WHERE email = '<that account>';`
3. **Sign in again.** The JWT is a snapshot of the role at sign-in time, so a token minted *before* the promotion still claims `USER` and every admin call answers **403**.
4. Now `POST /api/admin/seed` works, and `admin@yatra.com` / `Yatra@123` exists afterwards for everyone else.

**The cheaper way, if you have the signing key:** mint one admin JWT by hand and use it for that first seed. The token is an HS256 JWT signed with `yatra.jwt.secret` (the `local` profile reads it from `application-local.properties`) and the claims are the ones `JwtUtil` writes — `sub` (the numeric user id), `name`, `email`, `role: "ADMIN"`, `iat`, `exp`. Sign it, send it as `Authorization: Bearer …` to `POST /api/admin/seed`, and the seeded `admin@yatra.com` account exists from then on, so the sign-in request above works and nothing else needs hand-editing. That is how this collection's own live walk was bootstrapped.

Verified while writing this: against the current database, `POST /api/auth/login` as `admin@yatra.com` answers **401 `INVALID_CREDENTIALS`** — the live schema is not seeded right now, which is exactly this situation.

## Running the whole collection

**Work down the folders in order.** A request that needs an id reads it from a collection variable the previous folder's create filled in — the module folders are written as a single walk, not as twenty unrelated requests.

**A re-run leaves its own rows behind — that is the design, not a leak.** The run creates a flight, a booking, two airports and an airline; the booking holds a seat, so the flight can no longer be deleted and neither can the airline or the airports its route uses. *99 · Delete guards* runs those deletes on purpose to show the refusal, and `POST /api/admin/reset` deliberately does **not** remove rows the seeder did not create.

## Eight things worth knowing before you judge a red test

- **A booking's `status` is title case on purpose** (`Pending` / `Confirmed` / `Cancelled`), because `admin-bookings.js` compares those exact strings for its badge, its filter options and its cancel button — an uppercase body would silently colour every row red and hide the cancel action (risk R16 in the standards doc). Several tests here assert that vocabulary on purpose: if they fail, a page is about to break, not the test.
- **The write requests really do change rows.** `Confirm` / `Cancel` are the admin actions; `POST /api/admin/reset` followed by `POST /api/admin/seed` puts the demo dataset back exactly as it was — **in that order**, because `reset` only deletes and `seed` is what recreates. Give the reset a few minutes: it deletes row by row and takes roughly 80 seconds against the hosted database.
- **The creates invent their own codes** (`{{newIata}}`, `{{newCodeFrom}}`, `{{newFlightNo}}`) from the clock, so a second run does not 409 on the row the first one made. If one ever does collide (`409 IATA_EXISTS` / `DESTINATION_CODE_EXISTS` / `FLIGHT_NO_EXISTS`), edit that variable on the collection's **Variables** tab and resend — the request says so in its own failure message.
- **The payments folder answers with `bookings`, not `payments`.** `admin-payments.js` derives one transaction per *booking* and reads `resp.bookings`; a purpose-built payments array would leave that undefined and the page would quietly fall back to its localStorage demo seeds (risk R16). Relatedly, `outcome` in the verify body is a **mock-only** switch: a real gateway answers rather than being told.
- **One request is disabled by default:** *Upload a destination image* needs a file from your machine, so choose one in its form-data row and enable it. The Postman app honours that flag; a CLI runner (`newman`) does not, so its tests only register when a file is attached and a headless run reports it as skipped rather than red. Everything else runs as-is, and the destination creates work with no image at all (the empty string is a legitimate `imageUrl`).
- **The tickets folder carries two status filters, and they are two different columns.** `status` is the *booking's* vocabulary (`Confirmed` / `Cancelled`) — the dropdown `admin-tickets.js` really sends, where "Issued" and "Voided" are only its labels — while `ticketStatus` is the document's own `ISSUED` / `CANCELLED`. The refund the payments folder runs after the ticket is minted moves the payment row and nothing else, so this walk leaves an `ISSUED` ticket under a `Refunded` payment: the folder asserts that rather than assuming it.

- **The dashboard answers exactly two keys, and its cards are checked against other endpoints rather than against themselves.** `GET /api/admin/dashboard` is `{ bookings, stats }` — the recent-bookings rows and the seven §2.5 cards. When a dashboard test goes red, read the definition before the query: *Revenue* is the sum of `amount` over **non-cancelled** bookings (so a refunded booking still counts and a cancelled one does not), *Today's Bookings* counts bookings **created** today, and *Pending Payments* counts the booking's `paymentStatus` — not the payment row's `PENDING`. A money-first implementation is wrong here, not the test.

- **A query string has to be in the URL's *parameters*, not only in its `raw` text.** Editing `raw` in the JSON file is enough for the Postman app, which re-parses it whenever the request opens — but a CLI runner (`newman`) resolves the structured parts and sends **no** parameters at all. That is how one ledger request fetched the whole table instead of one transaction while the request itself still looked right in the app. Edit a URL by hand, edit its `query` array too.

The admin credentials below are the seeder's documented demo account (`SeedService.DEMO_PASSWORD`), not a secret — they exist so demo data nobody can sign into is not the demo data. See the standards doc, open question 8.

item.name: Admin · Airlines
item.description:
The airline module — the reference pattern every later admin module follows, and the only place where an image lives **inside** the database.

| Method | Path | Who |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/api/airlines`, `/api/airlines/{id}` | **public** — `searchFlight.js` renders an airline next to every flight card, signed out included |
| GET | `/api/airlines/{id}/logo` | **public** — bytes with a hash `ETag`, a day of public caching, and a `304` for a revalidating browser |
| POST / PUT / DELETE | `/api/admin/airlines…` | ADMIN, protected twice: the `/api/admin/**` route rule **and** `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` |

**The logo is not JSON.** No response body ever carries the Base64 blob — it carries `/api/airlines/{id}/logo`, the URL a page puts straight into `img.src`, which is why no page had to change when the mock was replaced (risk R8). The create below therefore sends a one-pixel PNG as a `data:` URL and the reads then fetch the bytes; if the image were serialised into the list body, every row would inflate by a third for data nothing reads.

**Run order inside this folder:** create → logo → list → get → update → logo again (same `ETag`, proving the echoed URL did not overwrite the image) → the three failure cases → a spare airline that exists only to show a real `DELETE` (`204`) and the `404` that follows it. The airline the flights folder needs is `{{airlineId}}` — do not delete that one; *99 · Delete guards* runs that delete on purpose to show the refusal.

The carrier the rest of this folder — and the flight in the next one — hangs off.

**Why the `logo` field holds a `data:` URL here.** The admin page's file button produces exactly that, and the API stores it verbatim: the logo is Base64 **in the `airline` table**, which is the literal reading of the brief's "store the image in the database". The one-pixel PNG below is a real, decodable image, so every request after this one exercises the true path — decode, sniff, hash, serve.

**`logo` means three things and the API knows which is which** (see the update request): a `data:` URL replaces the image, `""` clears it, and anything else is treated as *unchanged* — because the page stages the URL the API itself returned back into the form on any edit. Sending `""` on a create is the third case at rest: a new airline with no image, which still answers `logo: ""` rather than `null`.

The bytes endpoint, public because the storefront is. The Base64 in the database is decoded here and nowhere else, the media type comes from the data URL's own header (falling back to sniffing the first bytes when a bare Base64 string was stored), and the `ETag` is a SHA-256 of the decoded bytes — so it changes exactly when the image does.

**This is the endpoint a phase was lost to.** When the airline reads went live without it, every `img.src` pointed at a `401` and the storefront simply drew no logos — no error, no console noise. Hence the explicit `zero-auth` on this request: it must answer for a signed-out visitor, and the next request proves the `ETag` is not decorative.

request.description:
A replace, so every field is resent.

**The `logo` field here is the interesting one, and this request is deliberately the case that looks wrong.** `admin-airlines.js` stages the row's own `logo` value (the URL the API returned) back into the form on any edit where no new file was chosen. If the service stored that verbatim it would overwrite a real image with the string `"/api/airlines/3/logo"`, and the next logo read would try to Base64-decode a URL and fail. So a non-`data:`, non-blank value means **unchanged** — the middleware's decision, recorded in `AirlineService.apply`. The request after this one proves the bytes survived.

The trade-off is explicit: a malformed logo value is ignored rather than rejected, which is what keeps every existing page working.

item.name: Admin · Destinations
item.description:
The destination module — the second image pattern, built beside the airline logo so the contrast is demonstrable rather than theoretical.

| Method | Path | Who |

`POST /api/bookings` — wizard step 2, and the API's **only public write**.

item.name: 99 · Delete guards
item.description:
The rows this run created cannot all be removed again, and that is the modules working rather than failing.

Every delete in this API is guarded: a parent row that something still points at refuses, with a message that names what is holding it and says **disable it instead**. The flight this run created has a booking (the booking write), the airline has that flight, and the airport has that flight's route — so all three deletes answer `409` and the two writing rules below (`status: Inactive`) are the **actual** removal path: a flight that still exists for its bookings, but no longer appears to shoppers.

**Why `POST /api/admin/reset` does not clean this up either.** A reset removes the rows *the seeder* created, decided by a `seeded` marker column rather than by matching names — deliberately, so it can never take an admin's own flight with it. These rows carry no marker, so they stay. They are, in effect, the demo's evidence that the writes worked: open `admin-flights.html` and the flight is there.

**The pending booking has no HTTP delete at all.** `BookingService.deleteBooking` is the abandoned-booking path the seeder uses, and it refuses once a payment or a ticket exists (`409 BOOKING_HAS_SALE_RECORDS`) because a sale record is not a draft — the PNR and the gateway transaction id would go with it, and the payments page reads them. That is why the flight cannot be released: the honest answer to "how do I delete it" is `DELETE /api/admin/flights/{id}` **before** the booking exists, and the collection has already moved past that point on purpose.
